title: CHEST PAIN IN OPHTHALMIC PRACTICE: TRIAGE, TRAUMA & TRIUMPH
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide for ophthalmologists and emergency residents to navigate acute chest pain, from life-threatening post-operative pulmonary embolisms to atypical myocardial infarctions in surgical candidates.

sections.title: Core Definition & Classification
sections.content: In the context of ophthalmic practice and emergency medicine, acute chest pain is a critical symptom that necessitates immediate triage to distinguish life-threatening conditions from benign ones. Acute Chest Pain: Any new-onset discomfort or pain in the thorax that may indicate cardiac, pulmonary, esophageal, or musculoskeletal pathology.

rows: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS): Unstable Angina and Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI); Pulmonary Embolism (PE): Sudden blockage by thrombus; Aortic Dissection: Tearing of the aortic wall; Tension Pneumothorax: Air trapped in pleural space; Esophageal Rupture: Catastrophic GI event.

sections.title: Scenario 1: Acute MI in the Waiting Area
content: Scenario: 65yo male, smoker, HTN, clutching chest with 'squeezing' pain radiating to jaw/arm.
Immediate Action: Shout for help, Call cardiac arrest team (Emergency Code), Assess ABC.
Clinical Picture: Diaphoresis (sweating), pale, breathless.
Drug Doses: High-flow O2 (100%), Aspirin 300mg chewed, Sublingual GTN, Morphine 5–10mg IV + Metoclopramide 10mg IV.
Investigations: 12-lead ECG (ST elevation/Q waves), Cardiac Troponins, CK-MB.

sections.title: Scenario 2: Post-Op Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
content: Context: 75yo patient, 5 days post-vitrectomy (GA), sudden breathlessness + pleuritic pain.
Key Action: Call medical emergency team immediately (Do not wait for CXR if unstable).
Clinical Signs: Tachypnea (>20/min), tachycardia, hypotension, cyanosis.
Management: 100% O2, Morphine 10mg IV, immediate anticoagulation (LMWH or Unfractionated Heparin 10,000 U IV bolus).
Gold Standard: Spiral CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA).

rows: 25yo male, lid procedure, respiratory distress, tracheal deviation to right.
14–16G cannula in 2nd ICS, mid-clavicular line. DO NOT wait for CXR.
Tearing chest pain radiating to back/shoulder blades. Malignant HTN.
Urgent CT/MRI. Check unequal BP in arms. IV Phentolamine (2–5 mg) for BP crisis.

content.explanation: 80yo male, headache, jaw claudication. Large-vessel vasculitis involving aorta can lead to dissecting aneurysms or MI. Pathognomonic jaw claudication is highly predictive. Treatment: IV Methylprednisolone 1g/day for 3 days.

sections.title: Scenario 6 & 7: MI Masquerades & Angina
content: Inferior MI: Elderly/Diabetic presentation as 'indigestion' or epigastric discomfort. Look for ST elevation in II, III, aVF.
Stable Angina: Exertional pain relieved within 5 mins of rest.
Unstable Angina Red Flag: Pain at rest, >15 mins, or increasing frequency. Requires hospital admission.
Bruce Protocol: Exercise treadmill test; ST depression >2mm is significant.

branches: Pleuritic Pain: Sarcoidosis, GPA (Wegener's), or SLE
Cardiac Failure: TB, Sarcoidosis, or HIV

sections.title: Scenario 9 & 10: Cocaine & Shock
content: Cocaine: Causes intense vasospasm and sympathetic surge. Can lead to both Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) and MI. Manage: ED cardiac monitoring + Ocular massage/paracentesis.
Hypovolemic Shock (AAA): Patient with AAA becomes cold/clammy with chest/abdominal pain. Tachycardia + BP drop. Manage: Two 14–16G cannulae, 1L rapid crystalloid, urgent surgery.

sections.title: Scenario 11 & 12: Sarcoidosis & Anaphylaxis
content: Cardiac Sarcoidosis: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + mutton-fat KPs. Can cause conduction blocks/arrest. Screen with ECG and Echo.
FFA Anaphylaxis: Chest tightness + itching post-fluorescein. Manage: Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (1:1000). Repeat every 5 mins. Observe 48 hours for biphasic reactions.

rows: Butterfly rash, anterior uveitis, chest pain relieved by leaning forward.
ECG: Diffuse saddle-shaped ST-elevation. Treat with Steroids or NSAIDs.
Tall, high-arched palate, ectopia lentis, sudden excruciating chest pain.
Ruptured dissecting aortic aneurysm. Immediate cardiothoracic transfer.
3 days post-eye surgery, fever, cough, pleuritic pain.
Consolidation, bronchial breathing. Tx: Cefuroxime 1.5g IV + Clarithromycin 500mg IV.

branches: Immediate (Shout/Triage): Unresponsive? → CPR (30:2). Responsive? → ABC & O2.
Detailed Triage: Heavy? (ECG/ACS), Sharp? (DVT/PE), Tearing? (Dissection), Neck veins/Absent breath? (Tension PTX).
Interventions: Aspirin 300mg, Nitrates (unless low BP), Morphine 10mg IV.
Secondary: CXR (TB, Pneumonia), D-Dimer (Exclude PE), CTPA/CTA.

sections.title: Pearls, Pitfalls & Examiner's Picks
content: Pearl: In GCA, visual loss is permanent; steroids protect the fellow eye and prevent systemic MI/Stroke.
Pitfall: Do NOT give Nitrates if BP <90 mmHg; it worsens cardiogenic shock.
Examiner's Pick: Suspect PE if an elderly patient collapses 1–2 weeks after ocular surgery.
Precaution: Topical Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia tachycardia or worsen asthma-related chest pain.
High Yield: D-Dimer has high sensitivity but low specificity; best for EXCLUDING PE when negative.
Red Flag: Sudden 'worst headache of life' followed by chest pain suggests ruptured aneurysm with stress cardiac events.

data.generationPrompt:
In the context of ophthalmic practice and emergency medicine, acute chest pain is a critical symptom that necessitates immediate triage to distinguish life-threatening conditions from benign ones.
Definition & Classifications
Acute Chest Pain: Any new-onset discomfort or pain in the thorax that may indicate cardiac, pulmonary, esophageal, or musculoskeletal pathology.
Classifications of Chest Pain:
Life-Threatening:
Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS): Unstable Angina and Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI).
Pulmonary Embolism (PE): Sudden blockage of pulmonary circulation by a thrombus.
Aortic Dissection: Tearing of the aortic wall.
Tension Pneumothorax: Air trapped in the pleural space causing mediastinal shift.
Esophageal Rupture: Catastrophic gastrointestinal event.
Other Causes:
Pericarditis, pneumonia, pleurisy.
Gastro-esophageal reflux or esophageal spasm.
Musculoskeletal: Rib fractures, costochondritis.
Sickle-cell crisis.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OSCE & VIVA Clinical Scenarios
Scenario 1: Acute MI in the Waiting Area
Scenario: A 65-year-old male with hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history is waiting for his clinic appointment. He suddenly clutches his chest and reports severe "squeezing" retrosternal pain radiating to his left jaw and arm.
Answer:
Immediate Management: Shout for help, Call the cardiac arrest team (Emergency Code), and assess ABC.
Clinical Picture: Patient may be sweating (diaphoresis), pale, and breathless.
Treatment (Drug Doses):
High-flow Oxygen: 100% via face mask.
Aspirin: 300 mg chewed immediately.
Nitrates: Sublingual GTN (spray or tablet).
Morphine: 5–10 mg IV + antiemetic (e.g., Metoclopramide 10 mg IV).
Investigations: 12-lead ECG (look for ST elevation or pathologic Q waves), cardiac troponins, CK-MB.
Scenario 2: Post-Operative Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
Scenario: A 75-year-old patient 5 days post-vitrectomy surgery under general anesthesia reports sudden breathlessness and sharp, pleuritic chest pain that worsens with inspiration.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Suspected Pulmonary Embolism (PE).
Key Action: Call the medical emergency team. Do not delay for a CXR if the patient is unstable.
Clinical Signs: Tachypnea (>20/min), tachycardia, hypotension, and cyanosis.
Management: 100% O2, Morphine 10 mg IV for pain, and immediate anticoagulation with LMWH or Unfractionated Heparin (10,000 U IV bolus).
High Yield: Spiral CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the diagnostic gold standard.
Scenario 3: Tension Pneumothorax
Scenario: A thin, 25-year-old male presents for a minor lid procedure. He suddenly develops acute respiratory distress, chest pain, and his trachea is noted to be deviated to the right.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Tension Pneumothorax (Left side).
Threat: Rapidly leads to cardiorespiratory arrest due to compression of the great veins.
Management (Immediate): Insert a large-bore (14–16G) cannula into the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line on the affected side.
Pitfall: Do not wait for a CXR to confirm the diagnosis.
Scenario 4: Aortic Dissection
Scenario: A patient reports "tearing" chest pain that radiates directly to the back between the shoulder blades. He is known to have poorly controlled malignant hypertension.
Answer:
Clinical Finding: Pain is sharp and "tearing" rather than heavy/constricting.
Investigation: Urgent CT scan or MRI. Check for unequal blood pressure in both arms.
Management: Cautious lowering of BP using IV agents like Phentolamine (2–5 mg IV) in specific crises.
Scenario 5: Chest Pain and Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)
Scenario: An 80-year-old male with a history of headache and jaw claudication develops sudden chest pain.
Answer:
Key Points: GCA is a large-vessel vasculitis that can involve the aorta, leading to dissecting aneurysms or myocardial infarction.
Examiner's Pick: Pathognomonic jaw claudication is highly predictive of GCA.
Management: Immediate high-dose IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day for 3 days).
Scenario 6: Inferior MI masquerading as "Indigestion"
Scenario: An elderly lady scheduled for cataract surgery reports "indigestion" and epigastric discomfort rather than typical chest pain.
Answer:
Atypical Presentation: Elderly and diabetic patients often present with "silent" or atypical MI.
Management: Treat all epigastric pain in high-risk patients as cardiac until proven otherwise. Obtain an immediate ECG.
ECG Finding: Look for ST elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF).
Scenario 7: Stable vs. Unstable Angina
Scenario: A 60-year-old male reports chest pain only during exertion that is relieved within 5 minutes of rest.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Stable Angina.
Red Flag: If the pain occurs at rest, lasts longer than 15 minutes, or is increasing in frequency, it is Unstable Angina (part of ACS) and requires hospital admission.
Investigation: Exercise treadmill test (Bruce protocol); look for ST depression >2mm.
Scenario 8: Chest Pain as Systemic Review in Uveitis
Scenario: A VIVA examiner asks: "What systemic diseases associated with uveitis cause chest pain?".
Answer:
Pericarditis: Associated with Tuberculosis (TB), RA, or SLE.
Myocarditis: Associated with Syphilis.
Pleuritic Pain: Associated with Sarcoidosis, GPA (Wegener's), or SLE.
Cardiac Failure: Associated with TB, Sarcoidosis, or HIV.
Scenario 9: Cocaine-Induced Chest Pain and CRAO
Scenario: A young male presents with sudden vision loss (CRAO) and acute chest pain.
Answer:
Mechanism: Cocaine causes intense vasospasm and sympathetic surge, leading to both retinal artery occlusion and myocardial ischemia.
Management: Refer to the emergency department for cardiac monitoring and treat the ocular occlusion (e.g., ocular massage, paracentesis).
Scenario 10: Chest Pain in Shock
Scenario: During a clinic visit, a patient with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm becomes cold, clammy, and reports chest and abdominal pain.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Hypovolemic Shock (Ruptured aneurysm).
Vital Signs: Tachycardia (>100 bpm) and rapid drop in BP.
Management: Two wide-bore (14–16G) cannulae, rapid crystalloid infusion (up to 1L), and urgent surgical referral.
Scenario 11: Sarcoidosis and Cardiac Arrest
Scenario: A patient with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and mutton-fat keratic precipitates suddenly collapses with chest discomfort.
Answer:
Key Point: Cardiac sarcoidosis can cause conduction blocks and sudden cardiac arrest.
Investigation: Screening ECG and Echo are indicated for all ocular sarcoidosis patients.
Scenario 12: Anaphylaxis and Chest Pain
Scenario: Seconds after Fluorescein injection for FFA, a patient reports "tightness" in the chest and becomes itchy.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Anaphylactic Shock.
Management: Adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (1:1000). Repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement.
Precaution: Do not discharge for at least 48 hours due to risk of "biphasic" reactions.
Scenario 13: Chest Pain in SLE (Lupus)
Scenario: A 30-year-old female with a butterfly rash and anterior uveitis reports sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Pericarditis secondary to SLE.
Investigation: ECG showing diffuse ST-elevation (saddle-shaped).
Treatment: Systemic steroids or NSAIDs.
Scenario 14: Chest Pain and Marfan Syndrome
Scenario: A tall patient with high-arched palate and ectopia lentis presents with sudden excruciating chest pain.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Ruptured dissecting aortic aneurysm.
Key Finding: Marfan syndrome is a major risk factor for aortic root dilation and dissection.
Management: Immediate transfer to cardiothoracic surgery.
Scenario 15: Post-Operative Pneumonia
Scenario: Three days after eye surgery, a patient develops fever, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain.
Answer:
Diagnosis: Pneumonia.
Signs: Consolidation, dull percussion note, and bronchial breathing.
Management: Empiric antibiotics (e.g., Cefuroxime 1.5g/8h IV + Clarithromycin 500mg/12h IV).

Workup & Approach Mind Map (The "Chest Pain" Algorithm)
Immediate Assessment (The "Shout and Triage" Phase):
Unresponsive? → Start CPR (30:2).
Responsive? → Secure Airway, assess Breathing (O2 sats), and Circulation (BP/Pulse).
Detailed Triage:
Heavy/Squeezing? → ECG for ACS/MI.
Sharp/Pleuritic? → Look for DVT signs → PE.
Tearing/Back radiation? → Aortic Dissection.
Distended neck veins + Absent breath sounds? → Tension Pneumothorax.
Emergency Interventions:
Aspirin 300mg (ACS).
Nitrates (unless hypotensive).
Morphine 10mg IV.
Secondary Investigations:
CXR (TB, pneumonia, cardiomegaly).
D-Dimer (to exclude PE).
CTPA/CTA (Vessels).
Definitive Disposition:
Transfer to CCU/ICU.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Management Pearls & Pitfalls
Pearl: In GCA, visual loss is often permanent, but steroids are given to protect the other eye and prevent systemic MI/Stroke.
Pitfall: Do not give Nitrates to a patient who is hypotensive (BP <90 mmHg) as it may worsen cardiogenic shock.
Examiner's Pick: In the elderly, always suspect PE if they collapse 1–2 weeks after ocular surgery.
Precaution: Topical Beta-blockers for glaucoma can mask the tachycardia sign of hypoglycemia or worsen an asthma-related chest pain.
High Yield: A D-Dimer test has high sensitivity but low specificity; it is most useful for excluding PE when negative.
Red Flag: Sudden "worst headache of life" followed by chest pain suggests a ruptured aneurysm with secondary stress-induced cardiac events.
